record.title: Password changes leave other pre-change Account bearers usable
record.description: A holder of a copied, still-valid Account bearer can continue using it after the legitimate Account holder changes the password, for the remainder of the one-hour token lifetime. For the bootstrap Account, a bearer issued while mustChangePassword is true also becomes owner-capable when somebody else completes the password change. The source has no session-specific state that distinguishes the current caller's bearer from another holder's bearer. The candidate requires prior possession of a valid token and stops at authority within that Account's own Organization; it does not establish a way to obtain a token or gain deployment-wide administration.
record.claimed_root_cause: Account JWTs contain no session identifier or password epoch. setPassword changes only passwordHash and mustChangePassword, while AccountAuthGuard verifies the static signing key and current Account/Membership state without checking an issuance epoch or revocation state. Clearing mustChangePassword therefore affects every unexpired token for that Account, including separately held first-login tokens. Preserving the current password-changing session may be intentional, but this representation cannot invalidate other sessions separately.

trace.description: An Account login before the password change issues the bearer later held by the attacker. The attacker must already possess this valid token.
The bearer contains Account sub/email and a 3600-second expiry, with no session identifier or password-version binding.
The legitimate holder uses a separate session to change the Account password; the service verifies the current password before writing the new hash.
Only passwordHash and mustChangePassword are updated. No bearer-revocation state is changed.

The old bearer still passes signature/audience verification before expiry. The stored Account exists, and its current mustChangePassword false value removes the first-login restriction for all such bearers.
The stale bearer supplies the same Account id, whose existing owner Membership and same-Organization Project satisfy the otherwise correct authorization checks.
A holder of the pre-change token can create a new Project-bound OAuth client under the Account's Organization without knowing the new password.

evidence.description: Account token issuance binds only sub/email, static issuer/audience/key and one-hour expiration.
Changing the password correctly requires the current password, but the successful path does not revoke or rotate pre-existing bearer state.
The password write changes only passwordHash and mustChangePassword.
The strongest current-state controls reload Account and Memberships; they do not compare token issue time/version with the password change. The first-login gate uses the Account's current boolean.
Account has no session version, password-change time or revocation relation that the guard could consult.
The existing test expects a pre-change token to work after the root password change. This was read as source, not executed, and does not cover invalidating a separately held token.

blockers: A bounded two-session lifecycle check was not executed because the assignment prohibits target-controlled execution without complete OS memory and cumulative disk controls. The required local observation of stale-token authorization is therefore unavailable.

validation_plan.local: After the parent establishes the complete sandbox, create a dummy owner Account, its Organization and one dummy Project. Issue two bearer sessions at distinct controlled clock instants. Use the second session and the current dummy password to change the password, then try exactly one protected OAuth-client creation with the first bearer before its original expiry. Repeat the transition with a dummy bootstrap Account: verify the first bearer is blocked while mustChangePassword is true, change the password through the second session, then try that first bearer once. Stop at the first dummy client record or rejection. Do not exchange the resulting client secret, contact external services or use real credentials.
